steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our machine learning paper on learning from label proportions (LLP). Explain the LLP setting, the two sources of information we can use, the connection to decoding parity-check codes with belief propagation, our two-stage iterative method, and end with a numbered list of contributions and headline results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- What LLP is and why it matters now
- Two sources of information: bag proportions and covariate similarity; existing methods
- Our idea: pseudo labels, inspired by parity-check decoding in coding theory
- Proposed two-stage iterative algorithm (Figure 1)
- Contributions: (1) LLP as parity recovery + BP, (2) Aggregate Embedding loss, (3) iteration and results

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- What LLP is and why it matters now
  - renewed interest: privacy, leakage of sensitive info (cite)
  - binary setting: instances aggregated into bags, only label count per bag (proportion of 1 's); features of all instances available
  - weak supervision vs instance-level labels
  - goal: instance-wise predictor good on test distribution
- Two sources of information
  - bag level label proportions (given)
  - indirect: smooth true classifier gives similar labels to similar covariates / feature vectors; covariates given explicitly
  - existing: fit average soft scores of DNN over bag to bag proportion (cite)
  - other class: instance level loss with pseudo labeling (cite)
- Our idea
  - build on per-instance pseudo labels; use bag constraints + covariate similarity explicitly
  - coding theory for communication (cite): decode unknown message from parity checks over groups of bits
  - parity checks = redundancy against noise/corruption in channel
  - state of the art codes (cite) decoded with Belief Propagation (cite) on factor graph: message bits = variable nodes, parity checks = factor nodes (sum odd/even)
  - sum-product BP -> marginal soft score per bit
- Proposed algorithm
  - novel iterative, two stages: existing embedding -> pseudo-labels; pseudo labels -> refine embeddings; iterate
  - central approach in Figure 1
- Contribution 1
  - parallel LLP <-> parity recovery: labels = message bits, bag counts = parity checks (more general)
  - Gibbs distribution enforcing bag constraints
  - extra redundancy from covariates: pairs in K -nearest neighborhood forced to similar labels = another " parity constraint "
  - cartoon in step 1 of Fig. 1: neighbors -> similar labels (colors)
  - sum product BP -> marginal pseudo labels
  - first work connecting parity recovery and LLP (to our knowledge)
- Contribution 2
  - thresholded soft pseudo labels -> full supervision -> new embedding
  - problem: thresholded labels may violate bag constraints
  - DNN with 1) instance head (loss vs thresholded pseudo label), 2) bag level head pooling penultimate layer reps in bag (loss vs bag proportion)
  - Aggregate Embedding loss; trains penultimate layer embedding
- Contribution 3
  - iterate, previous embedding as features
  - beat LLP baselines incl. DLLP (cite) by wide margins
  - upto 15% UCI; upto 0.8% Criteo (large, hard); upto 7% images
  - large bag regime: upto 15% gains for bag size \geq 512
  - bag size 2048: max ~ 20 bags, no significant degradation
  - ablations: 1 -NN gets most gains vs k -NNs (Section A.1.1)
  - KNN constraints down to 50% -> significant drop (Section 6.2)
  - other ablations (Section 6, Section A.1)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Learning from Label Proportions (LLP) has gotten renewed interest recently, because of rising concerns about privacy and leakage of sensitive information. In the binary classification setting of LLP, all training instances are put together into bags and only the aggregated label count of a bag is available, i.e. the proportion of 1 's in a bag. The features of all the instances are available. This is a form of weak supervision compared to giving labels at the instance level. The main goal is to learn an instance wise predictor that performs very well on the test distribution.

There are two sources of information that can help predict the instance wise label on the training set. The first one is the bag level label proportions that are given to us. The second one is indirect, and it comes from the fact that any smooth true classifier would probably assign similar labels to instances with similar covariates or feature vectors. The covariate information of instances in the bags is given explicitly. Some current methods fit the average soft scores over a bag, predicted by a deep neural network (DNN) classifier, to the given bag label proportion. Another class of approaches trains a classifier on an instance level loss that is obtained with some kind of pseudo labeling.

Our work builds on the idea of making pseudo labels per instance. The key observation is that we can use two types of information, bag level constraints and covariate similarity information, in an explicit way. To do this we take inspiration from coding theory for communication systems. There, one of the fundamental problems is to decode an unknown message string sent by the encoder, using only parity checks over groups of bits from the message. The parity checks give redundancy that fights against noise/corruptions in the channel. The state of the art codes are decoded using Belief Propagation on a factor graph where the message bits are variable nodes (whose "label" has to be learnt) and the parity checks are factor nodes (that constrain the sum of bits in the parity check to be odd or even). Sum-product belief propagation is used to learn the marginal soft score on each of the message bits.

- Proposed algorithm: iterative, two stages (embedding -> pseudo-labels -> refine embedding, iterate); Figure 1
- Contribution 1: LLP <-> parity recovery; labels = message bits, bag counts = parity checks; Gibbs distribution with bag constraints; K -nearest neighbor pairs forced to similar labels (another " parity constraint "); Fig. 1 step 1 cartoon; sum product BP -> marginal pseudo labels; first to make this connection
- Contribution 2: thresholded soft pseudo labels for full supervision; may violate bag constraints -> DNN with instance head + bag level head (pooling penultimate reps); Aggregate Embedding loss trains penultimate embedding
- Contribution 3: iterate; beat baselines incl. DLLP; upto 15% UCI, upto 0.8% Criteo, upto 7% images; bag size \geq 512 upto 15%; bag size 2048 ~ 20 bags, no big degradation; 1 -NN vs k -NN (Section A.1.1); KNN constraints 50% -> drop (Section 6.2); other ablations (Section 6, Section A.1)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Learning from Label Proportions (LLP) has gotten renewed interest recently, because of rising concerns about privacy and leakage of sensitive information. In the binary classification setting of LLP, all training instances are put together into bags and only the aggregated label count of a bag is available, i.e. the proportion of 1 's in a bag. The features of all the instances are available. This is a form of weak supervision compared to giving labels at the instance level. The main goal is to learn an instance wise predictor that performs very well on the test distribution.

There are two sources of information that can help predict the instance wise label on the training set. The first one is the bag level label proportions that are given to us. The second one is indirect, and it comes from the fact that any smooth true classifier would probably assign similar labels to instances with similar covariates or feature vectors. The covariate information of instances in the bags is given explicitly. Some current methods fit the average soft scores over a bag, predicted by a deep neural network (DNN) classifier, to the given bag label proportion. Another class of approaches trains a classifier on an instance level loss that is obtained with some kind of pseudo labeling.

Our work builds on the idea of making pseudo labels per instance. The key observation is that we can use two types of information, bag level constraints and covariate similarity information, in an explicit way. To do this we take inspiration from coding theory for communication systems. There, one of the fundamental problems is to decode an unknown message string sent by the encoder, using only parity checks over groups of bits from the message. The parity checks give redundancy that fights against noise/corruptions in the channel. The state of the art codes are decoded using Belief Propagation on a factor graph where the message bits are variable nodes (whose "label" has to be learnt) and the parity checks are factor nodes (that constrain the sum of bits in the parity check to be odd or even). Sum-product belief propagation is used to learn the marginal soft score on each of the message bits.

Motivated by this connection, we propose a new iterative algorithm with two stages: we use an existing embedding to learn pseudo-labels and then we use the learnt pseudo labels to refine the embeddings, and we repeat this with the new embeddings. Our central approach is shown in Figure 1. Our contributions are below:

1) We draw a parallel between the LLP problem and the parity recovery problem, for pseudo labeling. The labels of the instances are the bits of the message and the parity checks are the bag level counts (which is more general than just parity). We adapt this analogy to form a Gibbs distribution that enforces the bag constraints. To get more redundancy we exploit covariate information: for every pair of instances that are in the K -nearest neighborhood of each other, we force their binary labels to be similar, so another " parity constraint " is added to the Gibbs distribution. In the cartoon in step 1 of Fig. 1 you can see the nearest neighbors induce similar labels (colors). Then we run sum product Belief Propagation (BP) to get marginal pseudo labels. As far as we know, ours is the first work to make this connection between the information theoretic approach of recovering messages from parity and the LLP problem.

2) In the second stage, the new thing is that we use thresholded soft pseudo labels to give full supervision to learn a new embedding. But we observe that after marginalization, thresholded soft labels may violate the bag constraints. So we use a new Deep Neural Network architecture that has 1) an instance head that gives an instance level loss with the thresholded soft pseudo label and 2) a bag level head, made by pooling the penultimate layer's representations of the instances in a bag, which gives a loss between the bag proportions and the predicted bag level proportion. We call the final loss the Aggregate Embedding loss. This loss is used to train the penultimate layer embedding.

3) We iterate the two steps above, using the embedding from the previous step as features. We show that our iterative two stage algorithm in the end produces instance level predictions that beat a number of LLP baselines, including DLLP, by wide margins. The improvements are upto 15% on standard UCI classification datasets. We beat the baselines by upto 0.8% on the large and challenging Criteo dataset and upto 7% on image datasets. Our methods mostly beat most baselines in the large bag regime (upto 15% gains for bag size \geq 512), where supervision is very weak. Note that for bag size 2048 there are only a maximum of ~ 20 bags on the datasets, and still our method does not show significant degradation in performance. Our ablations show that 1 -NN gets most of the gains compared to using k -NNs in the pseudo labeling step (Section A.1.1). Reducing the percentage of KNN constraints (to 50%) gives a significant drop in test metrics, which shows that the 'parity checks' from covariate nearness are important (Section 6.2). We give many other ablations that validate different parts of our approach (Section 6 and Section A.1).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Learning from Label Proportions (henceforth LLP) has seen renewed interest recently due to rising concerns about privacy and leakage of sensitive information [1,2,3,4,5,6]. In the LLP binary classification setting, all the training instances are aggregated into bags and only the aggregated label count for a bag is available, i.e. proportion of 1 's in a bag. Features of all instances are available. This can be seen as a form of weak supervision compared to providing instance-level labels. The main goal is to learn an instance wise predictor that performs very well on the test distribution.

There are two sources of information that can help in predicting the instance wise label on the training set. One is the bag level label proportions that are provided. The other is indirect and comes from the fact that any smooth true classifier would likely assign similar labels to instances with similar covariates or feature vectors. Covariate information of instances belonging to the bags is explicitly given. Some current methods [5,1] propose to fit the average soft scores over a bag, predicted by a deep neural network (DNN) classifier, to the given bag label proportion. Another class of approaches seeks to train a classifier on an instance level loss obtained using some form of pseudo labeling [7,3].

Our work builds on the idea of forming pseudo labels per instance. Our key observation is that one could utilize two types of information, bag level constraints and covariate similarity information, in an explicit way. To realize this, we take inspiration from coding theory for communication systems [8,9], where one of the fundamental problems is to decode an unknown message string sent by the encoder using only parity checks over groups of bits from the message. Parity checks provide redundancy that battles against noise/corruptions in the channel. The state of the art codes [8] are decoded using Belief Propagation [10] on a factor graph where message bits are variable nodes (whose "label" is to be learnt) and parity checks form factor nodes (that constrain the sum of bits in the parity checks to be odd or even). Sum-product belief propagation is used to learn the marginal soft score on each of the message bits.

Motivated by this connection, we propose a novel iterative algorithm with two stages: we use an existing embedding to learn pseudo-labels, then use the learnt pseudo labels to refine embeddings, and we iterate this procedure with the new embeddings. Our central approach is described in Figure 1. We outline our contributions in detail below:

1) We draw a parallel between the LLP problem and the parity recovery problem for pseudo labeling. The labels of instances are bits of the message and parity checks are the bag level counts (more general than just parity). We adapt this analogy naturally to form a Gibbs distribution that enforces the bag constraints. To obtain further redundancy, we exploit covariate information: for every pair of instances that are in the K -nearest neighborhood of each other, we force their binary labels to be similar, i.e. another " parity constraint " is added to the Gibbs distribution. As the cartoon depiction in step 1 of Fig. 1 shows, the nearest neighbors induce similar labels (colors). We then do a sum product Belief Propagation (BP) to obtain marginal pseudo labels. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to make this connection between the information theoretic approach of recovering messages from parity and the LLP problem.

2) Our novelty in the second stage is to utilize thresholded soft pseudo labels to provide full supervision to learn a new embedding. However, we observe that after marginalization thresholded soft labels may violate bag constraints. We therefore use a novel Deep Neural Network architecture that has 1) an instance head giving rise to an instance level loss involving the thresholded soft pseudo label and 2) a bag level head formed by pooling the penultimate layer's representations of instances within a bag, giving rise to a loss between bag proportions and predicted bag level proportion. We call the final loss the Aggregate Embedding loss. This loss is used to train the penultimate layer embedding.

3) We iterate the above two steps, using the embedding obtained in the previous step as features. We show that our iterative two stage algorithm finally produces instance level predictions that outperform a number of LLP baselines including DLLP [1] by wide margins. Improvements are upto 15% on standard UCI classification datasets. We outperform the baselines by upto 0.8% on a large, challenging Criteo dataset and upto 7% on image datasets. Our methods outperform most baselines in the large bag regime (upto 15% gains for bag size \geq 512) where supervision is very weak. Notably, on bag size of 2048 there are only a maximum of ~ 20 bags on the datasets, and yet our method does not display significant degradation in performance. Our ablations show that 1 -NN achieves most of the gains relative to using k -NNs in the pseudo labeling step (Section A.1.1). Reducing the percentage of KNN constraints (to 50%) registers a significant drop in test metrics, underscoring the importance of 'parity checks' from covariate nearness (Section 6.2). Many other ablations validate different components of our approach (Section 6 and Section A.1).

[2] Busa-Fekete et al. (2023) Robert Istvan Busa-Fekete, Heejin Choi, Travis Dick, Claudio Gentile, et al. Easy learning from label proportions. arXiv preprint arXiv:2302.03115 , 2023.
